subject: math
title: Shapes, Measurement, and Data
summary: A five-day hands-on sequence for describing positions and shapes, comparing and composing shapes, measuring attributes directly, and sorting and counting objects.

materials.name: Flat shape cutouts in varied sizes and orientations
Solid objects such as a ball, box, can, and cone
Paper and a thick pencil or crayon

days.title: Shapes Around and Beside Us
days.objective: I can name a flat shape and describe where it is.
adultSetup: Place circles, triangles, rectangles, squares, and hexagons in varied sizes and rotations around a small play area.
Do not organize or identify shapes by color because color is not the defining attribute.
days.textRecommendation: Choose a shape-search picture book that shows shapes in multiple orientations and everyday settings.

directions: Use a toy to act out above, below, beside, in front of, and behind.
Let the learner copy each position and say or point to the matching word.
Name a triangle by its three straight sides and corners even when it points sideways.
Describe its location using a complete position phrase, such as beside the box.
Rotate the triangle and explain why its name does not change.
Find and name shapes in several positions around the play area.
Ask the learner to place a named shape above, beside, or behind an object.
Compare a large and small example to confirm size does not change the shape name.
Complete four on-screen position and shape-name checks.
Then follow one adult direction that combines a shape and a position without a visual answer choice.
Give an adult two shape-and-position directions to follow, then check the result.
Use one shape and two contrasting positions at a time.
Trace the shape's sides and corners before naming it, then physically move it to each position.

masteryEvidence: Names common flat shapes across more than one size or orientation.
Accurately follows or gives at least two directions using position words.

days.title: Flat Shapes and Solid Shapes
days.objective: I can tell whether a shape is flat or solid and compare its parts.
adultSetup: Pair flat shape cutouts with safe solid objects, such as a circle and ball or rectangle and box.
Include examples that differ in color, size, and orientation.
days.textRecommendation: Choose an illustrated book about building or objects in a town and notice flat faces and solid forms in the pictures and environment.

directions: Review two flat shapes by tracing their boundaries.
Roll a ball and slide a box, then describe what happened.
Model that a paper circle is flat while a ball is solid and can be held from different sides.
Compare a square and rectangle by counting sides and corners and noticing what is alike and different.
Turn each example to show that orientation does not change its attributes.
Sort objects into flat-shape pictures and solid objects using touch and sight.
Compare two flat shapes by sides and corners.
Compare two solid objects by whether they roll, stack, or have flat faces without using behavior as the only definition.
Complete four on-screen shape-name, flat-or-solid, and shape-comparison checks.
Explain one answer using a side, corner, face, or solid-versus-flat attribute.
Find one solid household object and sketch one of its flat faces.
Contrast one flat cutout with one solid object the learner can handle.
Trace around the flat shape, then turn the solid object and feel more than one face or surface.

masteryEvidence: Classifies familiar examples as flat shapes or solid shapes.
Compares two shapes using at least one defining attribute rather than color or size alone.

days.title: Build and Compose Shapes
days.objective: I can build a shape and combine smaller shapes to make a larger shape.
adultSetup: Prepare building sticks, dough connectors, shape cutouts, and a clear workspace.
Create one model triangle and one picture made from two or more shapes.
days.textRecommendation: Choose a picture book with buildings, quilts, mosaics, or tangram-like illustrations that invite noticing shapes within larger pictures.

directions: Trace and count the sides of a triangle and rectangle.
Choose which sticks might build each outline.
Build a triangle from three sticks and connect each endpoint.
Join two triangles to make a larger shape and trace the new outside boundary.
Name both the small component shapes and the composed shape when it has a familiar name.
Build a square or rectangle from sticks and check its sides and corners.
Combine two or more cutouts to match a simple silhouette.
Separate the composition and find a different arrangement using the same pieces.
Complete five on-screen comparison, building, and composing checks.
Build or draw one named shape and make one larger picture from at least two shapes without copying the adult model exactly.
Design a shape creature or building and tell which shapes were combined.
Place sticks directly over a printed outline before building without the outline.
Use only two large cutouts and rotate one at a time until their edges meet.

masteryEvidence: Builds or draws a recognizable flat shape from its attributes.
Combines at least two simple shapes and identifies the parts within the composition.

days.title: Describe and Compare Measurements
days.objective: I can describe measurable attributes and directly compare two objects.
adultSetup: Choose pairs of objects that can be aligned for length, lifted safely for weight, or visibly compared for capacity.
Avoid pairs whose difference is too subtle to judge directly.
days.textRecommendation: Choose a read-aloud about size, growth, cooking, or construction and notice words such as longer, shorter, heavier, lighter, and holds more.

directions: Name two measurable attributes of a familiar object, such as length and weight.
Act out long and short with arm movements without assigning numbers.
Align two pencils at one endpoint before deciding which is longer.
Compare two safe objects by holding one in each hand and describing which feels heavier.
Explain that fair comparison uses the same attribute and a direct method.
Compare three object pairs for length after aligning their endpoints.
Compare one pair for weight and one pair for capacity using safe direct methods.
Ask the learner to state the attribute and comparison word for each result.
Complete five on-screen attribute and direct-comparison checks.
Choose two new objects, select one shared attribute, compare them directly, and explain the result.
Order three objects from shortest to longest by repeating pairwise direct comparisons.
Compare only length with two clearly different objects.
Align endpoints together and trace from the shared start to each endpoint before using longer or shorter.

masteryEvidence: Names at least one measurable attribute for a familiar object.
Directly compares two objects sharing that attribute and uses an accurate comparison word.

days.title: Sort, Count, and Describe Data
days.objective: I can sort objects into categories, count each group, and compare the groups.
adultSetup: Prepare ten to fifteen objects with at least two observable sorting attributes.
Make category labels with words and simple symbols so categories do not depend on color alone.
days.textRecommendation: Choose an information book with pictured categories, such as animals, foods, or vehicles, and discuss how the author groups information.

directions: Describe two attributes of one object.
Sort three sample objects into two adult-named categories and explain the rule.
Choose one clear sorting rule and place every object into exactly one category.
Count each category by touching each object once and record the totals with numerals or marks.
Compare the category counts using more, fewer, or the same number.
Sort a mixed collection together and let the learner name the category rule.
Recount after arranging each category in a line to check accuracy.
Resort the same objects by a different attribute and discuss how the data changed.
Complete six on-screen attribute, comparison, and sorting-and-counting checks.
Independently sort a small set, count each category, and state which has more, fewer, or the same number.
Draw a simple picture record with one mark per object in each category and ask an adult a comparison question.
Use six objects and two categories with an obvious rule.
Place category symbols above two rows, touch-count each row, and pair objects across rows before comparing totals.

masteryEvidence: Classifies a collection into named categories using a consistent rule.
Counts each category accurately and compares the category totals with appropriate language.
Explains that a new sorting attribute can organize the same objects differently.

accommodationNotes: Use spoken and visible labels for position, shape, attribute, and category words.
Provide large tactile shapes and safe easy-grip objects when helpful.
Accept pointing, eye gaze, object placement, signing, or spoken explanation when drawing or handwriting is not assessed.
Use size, texture, symbol, or position in addition to color so no task requires color discrimination.

review.notes: Machine-validated instructional draft. It requires named human curriculum review before production use.
